# Results — Study 358 ("Watches are an asset class")

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Do Rolexes beat the S&P? We
test the strongest tradable version of the luxury-watch-as-investment claim: a secondary-
market **resale index** (hardcoded, cited, **approximate** — a labelled proxy, not a live
feed) and the only **listed** ways to buy the trade (Watches of Switzerland `WOSG.L`,
Richemont `CFR.SW`), each benchmarked against `SPY`. Offline & deterministic; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Resale index | **Hardcoded, cited, approximate** annual secondary-market level (base 100 @ 2018-12-31), reconstructed from public WatchCharts / Morgan Stanley×WatchCharts / press reporting — see [`docs/references.md`](references.md). **A PROXY, not a feed.** |
| Equity proxies | `WOSG.L` (Watches of Switzerland, LSE) · `CFR.SW` (Richemont, SIX) — month-end Adj Close via yfinance, cached under `_cache/` |
| Benchmark | `SPY` (month-end Adj Close, yfinance) |
| As-of | 2025-12-31 (month-end; no partial-year bar) |
| Equity window | 2019-01 → 2025-12 (CFR/SPY: 84 months; WOSG.L from its 2019-05 IPO: 80 months) |

> **Why proxies, stated as a decision.** Real secondary-market watch indices
> (WatchCharts Overall Market Index, the Subdial50, the Morgan Stanley×WatchCharts
> review) are **not freely API-available**. Rather than fabricate a live tape we (a)
> hardcode a small, clearly-cited, **approximate** annual series whose *shape* — a
> 2019–21 melt-up, a **March-2022** blow-off top, and a 2022–24 round-trip — is the
> load-bearing public fact, and (b) test the **tradable** equity proxies a public
> investor can actually buy. A retailer's and a conglomerate's equity are **not** the
> resale price of a steel Daytona; they are labelled proxies throughout.

## Half 1 — did the watches beat the S&P? (resale index vs SPY)

The (approximate, cited) secondary-market index, year-end levels base 100:

| year | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| level | 100 | 112 | 130 | **196** | 168 | 150 | 141 | 148 |
| YoY | — | +12.0% | +16.1% | **+50.8%** | −14.3% | **−10.7%** | −6.0% | +5.0% |

The reported **blow-off top was March 2022** (≈ level 220 on this scale); from there to
the 2024 low the index **round-tripped −35.9%**. Headline risk/return vs SPY:

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Resale watch index** | **+5.76%** | 22.2% | 0.34 | **−28.1%** |
| SPY (year-end) | **+15.03%** | 17.5% | — | −18.3% |

**The watches lost the race outright:** ~6%/yr vs ~15%/yr for the S&P, with *more* vol
and a *deeper* drawdown. The mean annual excess (index − SPY) is **−9.5%/yr**, **t = −1.05**
(p = 0.34, n = 6 years) — i.e. it underperformed, but with only 6 annual observations the
gap isn't even statistically *clean*; the honest read is "no evidence watches beat stocks,
and the point estimate is a large negative."

## Half 2 — the tradable proxies vs SPY (the only thing you can buy)

Monthly Adj Close, Newey-West (6-lag) alpha vs SPY. **These are labelled proxies.**

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max DD | alpha/yr | beta | NW *t*(α) | p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **WOSG.L** (retailer) | +6.76% | **55.2%** | 0.41 | **−77.0%** | −11.2% | 2.05 | −0.70 | 0.49 |
| **CFR.SW** (Richemont) | +17.07% | 32.8% | 0.64 | −36.3% | +3.9% | 1.04 | +0.41 | 0.68 |
| SPY | +16.06% | 16.7% | **0.98** | −24.0% | — | — | — | — |

Neither proxy shows a *significant* alpha vs SPY (|t| < 1 both ways). Watches of
Switzerland is a high-beta (β≈2) retailer that fell **−77%** peak-to-trough as the bubble
deflated — *more* exposed to the round-trip, not a hedge. Richemont roughly *matched* SPY's
return at twice the volatility and a worse Sharpe. **No harvestable alpha in either.**

## Half 3 — the carry/illiquidity haircut (what flipping really costs)

The pitch never charges the friction. A buy-high / sell-at-a-wholesale-discount round trip
costs ~**20%** (dealer margin + grey-market discount), amortised over a ~**3-year** hold,
plus ~**1%/yr** insurance/storage/servicing. Charged once on the index's gross CAGR:

| | value |
|---|--:|
| gross CAGR (index) | +5.76%/yr |
| − dealer-spread drag (20% over 3y) | −7.17%/yr |
| − insurance/storage carry | −1.00%/yr |
| **= NET CAGR a real flipper earns** | **−2.80%/yr** |

The 5.8% gross *that already lost to the S&P* turns **negative** once you pay to actually
transact and hold the metal. T-bills beat it; the S&P laps it.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic, fixed-seed "bubble-and-round-trip" path (planted boom CAGR +55%, bust
−30%, σ = 5%/mo, seed 358): the inference engine recovers the planted up-sign and a finite
Sharpe — peak ≈ 1015 → end ≈ 313, recovered CAGR **+15.9%**, Sharpe 0.81, max DD −69%,
`sign_ok = 1`. The harness can bank a planted signal, so a null on the real proxies is a
real null, not a broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE (it *under*-performs).** Over 2018–2025 the resale index returned
  ~6%/yr vs ~15%/yr for SPY; the annual excess is **−9.5%/yr (t = −1.05)** — no evidence
  watches beat stocks, and the point estimate is sharply negative. The proxies show **no
  significant alpha** (|t| < 1). The "watches are an asset class that beats the S&P" claim
  fails on the tape it's quoted on.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even the gross index CAGR (5.8%) goes **negative (−2.8%/yr)**
  after a realistic dealer-spread + carry haircut; the buyable proxies are higher-vol,
  deeper-drawdown beta (WOSG.L −77%, β≈2) with no alpha. Illiquid, high-carry, and a
  bubble that round-tripped 2022–2024.
- **"Watches beat the S&P?" — BUSTED.** On return, risk-adjusted return, drawdown *and*
  net-of-cost, the S&P wins every column. The few who "made money" bought before March
  2022 and sold near the top — survivors of a bubble, not an asset class.

> **Caveat (named, not buried).** The resale index here is a **small, hardcoded,
> approximate** reconstruction of public reporting — its *level path/shape* is defensible
> but its precise year-end values are not a live feed, and the annual *t* rests on just 6
> observations. The equity proxies are exactly that — proxies for "owning the watch trade,"
> not the resale price of a watch. Both limitations push the verdict toward humility, not
> toward a stronger claim: nothing here says watches beat stocks, and several lines say the
> opposite.
